item.title: Intro to Math Concepts for Game Design
item.description:
Because we will be rendering objects and systems into a digital screen, it is useful to understand a bit about Cartesian Coordinate Systems. The name is derived from Renee Descarte, famous french Thinker and Mathematician, and is the groundwork foundation for just about every foundational subject we're going to be talking about with the math going into Game Design. The basics of it is pretty simple. When indicating placement along a line, you can value points as discrete distances from one another. For instance, with the above line, we can say that the distance between 0 and 2 is, in fact, a value of | 2 |. In math terms, this is pretty easy to equate out. You take any two points, A and B, and subtract A from B ![[1Dline Distance.png]] This seems awfully rudimentary. Why even bring it up at all? In one dimension, as pictured above, things are easy to parse out. We can look at the line and objectively be able to eyeball the distances that things are spaced apart from each other. If we were to interpolate this line over into the 1000's, we could still use very basic mathematics to determine precise distances between two different points. There's two elements where this gets tricky - when we start to move into multiple dimensions and when we get into more precise calculations using decimal points. When we start to move into a multi-axis Cartesian Units, we're going to have to talk about the way digital screens render out. In your traditional math class, you will have this kind of crossed-axis set up:
Each one of the quadrant represents X and Y values in either ascending or descending values, running along both positive and negative values. Notice how Y behaves as it should naturally, with ascending values corresponding to positive Y values. Digital screens play a little differently
Digital Screens start rendering in the upper left hand corner and then ascend both X to the right and increase Y descending downward. The point where they meet in the upper left is called the origin point and is critically important to understanding how things are not only placed within any given scene, but also how objects are produced. Let's take a look at how this works in practice. Here let's introduce Daryl.
Daryl wants to move to the bottom right corner of the screen. Now, to our eyes, we would naturally need to increase the X value to make him move to the right. That makes sense! But because Daryl is rendered onto a digital screen, we will need to take Daryl's Y position and, instead of subtracting him to move DOWN, we will need to add to his Y value to make him move in the intended direction. It is odd! And almost on purpose. It is important to know how to quantify 2D coordinate positions so that we can communicate with our digital screen where a thing is not only starting, but how to move it to where we need it to go.
For instance, Daryl has an X and Y coordinate that he starts on. This is quantified as: The Dot that he is moving towards always has an (X,Y) position. For argument's sake, let's give each of these objects some arbitrary values:
How far would Daryl have to travel in order to get from his position to the position of the dot? We already know how to do this with 1D math: But how do we calculate this when we have two X and two Y values? We can borrow another formula: ![[Pasted image 20260518131514.png]]
What this formula gives is something pretty far fetched and seems pretty inaccurate. It can give you a good idea of the distance between two differnt points, but a straight line is always going to be faster. Thats where 2D Trigonometry comes into play!
